paras: The Las Vegas jail attack of 1882 was an attempt by a crowd of about 100 to 150 men to break into the jail at Las Vegas, New Mexico Territory, in the early hours of July 12, 1882, and hang the prisoner H. C. Brown, accused of killing the butcher Frank Mayer. Sheriff Romero's guard fired on the crowd from the jail and drove it off, and a fourteen-year-old in the crowd, Eddie Brown, later died of his wounds. Wire reports carried the repulse across the country as the work of a mob of Germans avenging one of their own.

Frank Mayer, a 49-year-old German butcher, had earlier had his employee H. C. Brown convicted of stealing a dressed beef, and Brown, released a few days before, was reported to have made threats against him. On the night of July 10 a witness at the inquest testified that he saw Brown come up behind Mayer near Reidlinger's saloon and strike him on the head, and Mayer died soon after. On July 11 a coroner's jury under Justice of the Peace Jose Montoya found that Mayer died 'by a blow inflicted on him by a certain H. C. Brown', and Mayer was buried that afternoon.

Threats to lynch Brown circulated on the streets on July 11, and at about nine that night notices called a meeting of 'the vigilantes' at the southwest corner of the plaza. By midnight 100 to 150 men had gathered and drifted toward the jail at the northwest corner of the plaza, and the Gazette's reporter judged many of them to be onlookers, with women among the throng. Organizers had a greased rope tied in a noose, masks, and a heavy beam to serve as a battering ram.

Sheriff Romero, criticized after an earlier jail breaking, waited inside with Deputy Sheriff N. Segura and fifteen guards. At half past twelve a disguised leader gave the word, and the crowd struck the new jail door three times with the beam without breaking it. At the fourth blow the guards fired from the top of the jail wall, some in the crowd returned pistol shots, and four men fell before the crowd fled to the plaza carrying its wounded.

The Gazette named three of the wounded: Eddie Brown, a fourteen-year-old who kept a confectionery stand, shot twice in the right leg; Fred Neebold, a butcher, whose leg bone was shattered; and Jim Thora, hit in the instep. The next morning the street before the jail was marked by bullet holes and blood.

Eddie Brown, son of a Gazette compositor, died at 1:30 a.m. on July 15, and the Gazette printed an obituary calling him 'one of the victims of tho late shooting at the jail'. Neebold's leg was reset by three doctors, and by July 23 he and Thora were reported to be recovering. On August 23 the Gazette noted that Brown's trial for the murder of Frank Meyer had been continued to the next term of court, and no report of its result or of any charges against members of the crowd was found.

The Las Vegas Daily Gazette gave the attack a long eyewitness report under the headline 'A Terrible Night', calling the crowd 'a motley one, composed of all classes and all races' and treating the presence of women from 'the dens of iniquity' as a sign of depravity. At the same time the paper described Brown as the man 'who had so cruelly beaten' Mayer and gave its sympathy to the family of the boy who was killed.

A short Las Vegas dispatch, relayed through Denver, ran from Sacramento to Portland, Maine, under headlines such as 'Lynchers Repulsed', describing the attackers as 'a mob of Germans, friends of Frank M. Mayer' and Brown as his murderer. Weekly digests in Minnesota, Dakota and Mississippi filed it among the week's crimes, one remarking that the mob had meant to initiate Brown 'into trapeze performing' and others adding that the sheriff had given 'ample warning'. The Morristown Gazette in Tennessee reprinted Eddie Brown's obituary, and other small papers repeated the digest item into late July.

Chicago's German-language Illinois Staats-Zeitung gave the fullest outside account, praising the dead Franz Meyer, calling Brown a scoundrel, and reporting that local indignation had turned on the sheriff for not first firing blanks. No paper in the coverage gave the race of Brown or of the wounded men.

The prisoner appears as H. C. Brown in the coroner's verdict and most dispatches, as B. C. Brown in other wire copies, and as W. G. Brown in the Staats-Zeitung. Wire reports said four were badly wounded and two would die, while the later Gazette reports recorded one death and two recoveries. The digests said the sheriff gave ample warning before firing, a point the Gazette's eyewitness account does not mention, and the Staats-Zeitung reported that he was blamed for not firing blanks first.

reader.title: Las Vegas jail attack of 1882
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd summoned by vigilante notices tried to batter in the jail door to hang the prisoner Brown and was driven off by the sheriff's guard (A1, A4, A13); this is an attempted lynching, with no report that the target was Black.

The intended victim, H. C. Brown, was not killed: the crowd of 100-150 failed to break the jail door and retreated under the guards' fire (A1, A4); the only death, Eddie Brown, was a member of the crowd shot by the sheriff's guard (A1, A11), so this was an attempted lynching.

The local Las Vegas Daily Gazette account (A1) and the independent Las Vegas wire dispatch (A4, A7) and German-language account (A18) agree that a mob attacked the jail to lynch Brown and was repulsed by gunfire.

accounts.label: Local newspaper (Las Vegas Daily Gazette)
accounts.gist: A Gazette reporter at the scene described vigilante notices, a mixed crowd of 100-150 including many onlookers and women, a disguised leader, a battering ram, and a volley from above the jail wall that brought down four men.

accounts.label: Las Vegas wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of Germans, friends of the murdered man, attacked the jail to lynch Brown; the guards badly wounded four, two of whom would die.

accounts.label: Weekly news digests
accounts.gist: A party of Germans tried to batter down the jail doors; the sheriff gave ample warning before the guards opened with Winchester rifles; a second attempt was predicted.

accounts.label: Illinois Staats-Zeitung
accounts.gist: A crowd 'mostly Germans' tried to lynch W. G. Brown for killing the well-liked butcher Franz Meyer; the guards fired three volleys, and local indignation turned against the sheriff for not firing blanks first.

framing.detail: The Gazette headlined 'A Terrible Night', called the crowd 'motley' and its presence a sign of 'depravity', while presenting the mob's target as the man who had 'so cruelly beaten' Mayer and mourning Eddie Brown.
Distant papers ran the brief 'Lynchers Repulsed' dispatch calling Brown Mayer's murderer and the attackers 'friends' of the dead man.
Weekly crime digests listed it among the week's 'Murderous Deeds', one joking about 'trapeze performing'.
The German-language Staats-Zeitung called Brown a 'Hallunken' and reported indignation at the sheriff for the bloodshed.

info: Night of July 11-12, 1882; the attack on the jail began at 12:30 a.m.
The jail at the northwest corner of the plaza, Las Vegas
Target: prisoner H. C. Brown (also 'B. C.' and 'W. G.' Brown), unharmed. Shot by the guards: Eddie Brown (James Edward Browne, 14), who died July 15; Fred Neebold, butcher; Jim Thora.

Brown was accused of killing Frank Mayer (Meyer), a 49-year-old German butcher, with a blow on the night of July 10; a coroner's jury on July 11 found Mayer died 'by a blow inflicted on him by a certain H. C. Brown'.
A crowd called by vigilante notices, led by a disguised leader and a 'central committee'; the Gazette called it 'all classes and all races', wire reports called it a mob of Germans, friends of Mayer.
The crowd retreated to the plaza carrying its wounded; Brown remained in jail.
